$comment: The load gate's declared limits. Judged by scripts/assert-load-baseline; produced by
scripts/test-load. Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-02-f4-pr-e-load-test-foundations-design.md.
EVERY NUMBER HERE IS MEASURED, NOT CHOSEN. `observed` records what real runs produced on the
rig in `measuredOn`; `max` is the worst of those with the headroom stated per row. A ceiling
invented at a desk is either so loose it gates nothing or so tight it fires on the first PR,
and there is no way to tell which without measuring. data-api.md sets the same precedent for
the filter budgets: 'The two term/candidate numbers are measured rather than chosen.'
THE GATING STATISTIC IS `min`, NOT p95, AND THAT WAS MEASURED TOO. On the first gate run every
p95 landed within 8-9 ms of every other -- ratios of 0.97 to 1.03 across shapes that plainly do
different work -- while `min` separated them cleanly. At this volume p95 is dominated by
scheduling and container-network jitter, not by the query. p95 is still measured and printed on
every row, and the calibration tier publishes it (docs/performance.md), because it is the
number F4's definition of done asks for. It just does not gate.
THIS FILE IS A MOVED-GOALPOST SURFACE. A red gate can be made green by editing it, which is the
same hazard a *.verified.* snapshot carries -- so .claude/hooks/turn-review-gate treats it as a
judged baseline and dispatches alvo-snapshot-judge when it moves. Move a ceiling only in the
same PR as the change that caused it, and say in the PR why the feature is worth the number.

count_exact.measuredOn: gate tier, 20k rows, Apple M-series + Docker Desktop, generator co-resident, 2026-09-02
count_exact.why: Prefer: count=exact is documented as one extra statement over the matching set (#110, #179). A breach means it stopped being one -- an N+1, or a count that no longer reuses the filter.

page_deep.measuredOn: gate tier, 20k rows, cursor walked to the tenant's last page (depth ~10k), 2026-09-02
page_deep.headroom: roughly 2x over the worst observation, deliberately wider than the others because #100's growth is documented as sublinear but UNBOUNDED and the depth reached scales with the tier
page_deep.why: #100: on a multi-term sort the keyset predicate is a nested disjunction and per-page cost grows with cursor depth. This pins how much. The denominator is the same sort shape at depth zero, which is what isolates depth from sort width.

sort_nullable.why: #178: a nullable sort key renders a portable CASE rank that no index on the key can serve, where a required key renders no rank at all. When the per-dialect native NULLS FIRST/LAST fix lands this number should collapse toward 1.0, and the ceiling should follow it down in that same PR.

row_policy.why: The same URL answered for a caller whose list rule carries `assigned_to == @user.id` (indexed), against one with no row predicate at all. One variable changes, so this is the rule engine's cost in the hot path -- and it is security-core surface, so it is the ratio to watch hardest.

select_projection.headroom: a tripwire against the value going UP, not a claim that it is low
select_projection.why: RECORDED, NOT DEFENDED. `select` is applied to the response, not to the SELECT list, so ~1.0 is the correct value today and it proves nothing (#117). It is kept because it is the instrument that will DEMONSTRATE the fix: when the port gains a projection member the number drops below 1.0 and the improvement is measured rather than asserted.

$comment: A breach needs BOTH the factor AND the absolute floor, and both numbers come from measuring
the SAME code twice. Across two interleaved arms of identical images, min varied by up to
1.5x (read_by_id 0.71-1.07 ms, list_indexed 1.57-2.27 ms, openapi 2.44-3.97 ms). A factor of
1.4 would therefore have fired on noise; 1.8 sits above the observed spread and still catches
anything that doubles.
STATED HONESTLY: at 20k rows every absolute latency is small, so the FLOOR is what usually
decides. That makes the absolute half a coarse tripwire for regressions larger than a few
milliseconds, and the ratios above the sensitive instrument. That division is the design's,
not an accident of these numbers.

read_by_id.why: The whole per-request floor: middleware, API-key auth, tenant resolution, policy resolve (#118), one keyed read. Measured 0.7-1.1 ms at the gate tier.

list_indexed.why: The reference shape, and the analysis's own criterion (baas-analyza.md:142). Every ratio is anchored on it, so a regression here moves everything. Measured 1.6-2.3 ms at the gate tier.

create.why: Validation, the unique check, the audit stamp and the outbox insert. A wider floor than a read because a write's variance is genuinely higher -- its p99 ran to 43 ms where its min was 2.3 ms.

openapi.why: #126 was an O(N^2) name scan with 6N set allocations per request, fixed in PR-D; this guards its return. The widest factor of the four, because min for a large JSON document is dominated by serialization scheduling: identical images measured 2.44 ms and 3.97 ms in the same job.
